questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: It was crucial for my choice to study af University of Leeds that the academic opportunities were of the highest standard and within a field of study and interest which could not be fulfilled by studying electives in Denmark or at University of Copenhagen.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: The university made it quite easy to gain access to the relevant information about my first week in Leeds. Some information about schedules were a bit more complicated, but the administration at the university was very welcoming and helped answer every question.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I was picked up, alongside some other international students at the Manchester Airport. They driver drove us straight to our accommodation. It was great as it both saved us time and trouble with public transport and suitcases.

I arrived at a Saturday, so my accommodations office was unfortunately closed, which made it a bit more difficult to move in.

The first week I had an introduction and meeting with our tutor at my school (I was connected to two schools, so I ended up attending only one orientation), which made sure I understood the academic system and some of the challenges most commonly faced by international students.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Orientation happened after the first classes, so some of the information would have been great to have before, but it worked nonetheless very well.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: University of Leeds has great network of residences for first year students and international students. It was very easy to apply and the fact that there was a housing guarantee made moving abroad less stressfull.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
Living in residences are much different than living on your own and the standards of living can differ greatly from residence to residence. I found it a bit difficult in the beginning to live in a residence with only undergrads and first year students, as on my postgrad I was a bit older.

Residences can be very social in all the best ways - check up on your residence on the reviews and what kinds of values are presented. Some are more social than others while some have more rules than others. Different residences cater to different kinds of students.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: As I had a bachelors in social science I was eligible for studying at different schools, which I could choose from. At Leeds you apply for 'discovery modules' - also known as electives, and then you can write why you are qualified for this specific course, if the course is not within your assigned school (as a postgrad in Sociology, I could study all electives connected to the School of Sociology and Social Policy, but I was also accepted into electives at School of Political Science and School of Philosophy), as I had relevant prerequisite course before applying.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The administration was available over email or call, and the answering time was very short compared to my home institution.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got into the classes that I wanted - I got accepted into more classes than I had time for, so I had to prioritise them.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I would advice future students to seek out what other courses other Schools have than necessarily the one you are connected to via your home institution. Some of the most interesting and thought provoking courses I had was completely different than what I would 'normally' study.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
In the postgraduate program in Sociology and the host university, there were no available courses for me to take so I did undergrad electives in sociology, criminology, and political theory.

I found the academic level adequate, yet the culture of teaching is less theoretical and more historical than what I am used to. The reading were of a good level and the theoretical discussion in the tutorials were of a good academic level.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The style of teaching is very different than Copenhagen. It is much more dialogue based and less 'using this theoretical stance one could argue this or that' and much more your personal engagement, understanding and opinion about theories. This was both fun, challenging and sometimes frustrating. 

I loved the amount of tutorials or "øvelsestimer" we had at Leeds - engaging and preparing for discussions with the actual professor was very rewarding and adding to my understanding of both the theories and the subject. I loved the use of open office hours to engage with the assignments and the work I was doing throughout the semester.

The examinations were also, for my schools, theoretical essays, which for me was very different from the more empirical and methodological approach at Institute of Sociology. at UCPH

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
State Crime and Immorality - Crimes of the Powerful.

Global Terrorism and Violence.

Reimagining Politics - Gender, Race, and Popular Culture.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would really recommend the courses "State Crime and Immorality" and "Reimagining Politics" as they both helped develop a more nuanced and critical view of modern society and institutions. 

I really enjoyed the course "Global terrorism and Violence", but I know that this is purely of a professional interest in democracy and political violence.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: While I knew that exchange would cost, I spend more money on travels around the UK, going on day trips, going to social activities and eating out than I would normally do - everyday is filled with activities or opportunities. I do not regret a pound spend.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
When getting a railcard (DO IT) public transportation on the trains around the UK was far less expensive than I imagined. Going out to eat or for drinks is less expensive than in Copenhagen and a lot of social activities are either cheap or free. 

I did not expect housing to be as expensive as it was - Leeds especially is an expensive city to live in, but overall there is a housing crisis in the UK.

Many of the everyday expenses are overall the same as in Denmark - groceries and necessities. There are money you can save by buying budget brands.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There are so many great societies and opportunities for engaging and meeting new people - for more that what I dared hope for before starting by exchange program.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Anything you can imagine. 

I was a part of the surf society, kickboxing, book club and knitting club. I attended activities at the debate club, went weekly to a jazz club, was at culture nights, took jewellery making classes and pottery painting with other students. The bars around and on campus have football screenings, pub quizzes, folk music nights and so much more.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I really recommend joining a few societies (there is a sign up fee, which can vary from £5 to £30, and while this can seem a lot, there is often a 'social' or activity once a week). It is a great way of meeting both other internationals but especially other British people - they can seem quite shy in class until you meet them outside class and they are suddenly the chattiest.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Living in the North and in West Yorkshire you have the perfect location for experiencing some of the most beautiful natural landscapes, hiking routes and scenery in England. It is also perfect for going around the North, into Scotland or even down south to London, Bristol, Oxford or the like.

I really recommend all the hiking routes around as well as the cutest British villages around Leeds - they are straight out of a Barnaby episode. Cities such as Harrogate, Harewood, York, and Hebden Bridge are absolutely stunning (and with a rail cars between €2-10 to go by train.)

Pack a pair of good walking boots and hike around the Moors of the Peak- and Lake Districts, walk alongside the cutest sheep you'll ever see and finish up in a tea house with a cuppa of Yorkshire Tea and a scone.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
Once you accept that the Northern English accent is just rubbish, you'll get on grand. The people in Yorkshire are so sweet and polite it is almost 'scary' in the beginning. Soon you'll learn to always greet other in shops and chatting up people in the queue. 

The university and the community of other internationals made the adjustment easy for me, and the university does focus a lot on events for internationals exactly to make sure we process any culture shock.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join the societies, chat up people in the bar and go where the locals go. Northerners are great at being hospitable and never once was I rejected when I asked "Do you guys mind if I join?".

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
The food was a big challenge for me as a Dane and bread-lover. The quality of food in the supermarkets and at the bakeries took some getting used to. The culture for eating quick and ready made food was a surprise and the amount of sugar and crisps certainly added a one or two pounds of the hips.

Leeds is a student city with many bars and pubs so I did find that drinking (or at least going out, wether you drink or not) was a part of socialising in the beginning. The famous "Otley Run" is a 17-bar-long pub-crawl dressed up in costumes - and you don't just do it once. So seeing Mario and Luigi on a Saturday afternoon running around campus or the surrounding are not uncommon - but quite funny.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I loved the mentality and friendliness of the people in Leeds, both the students, faculty or just the people you meet in the train or in the grocery store.   As a Dane, the chattiness was in the beginning quite strange, but I have come to love it and I try to incorporate it in my life in Copenhagen now.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
- Sometimes you have to invite yourself along - it people will definitely not mind you doing so
- Everyone is very young. Most people are in their very early twenties and that can cause some frustrations if you are 25 and have lived on our own.
- Take this as an opportunity to engage with your professor in 1:1 - use your tutorials and office hours to really understand and maybe learn even more than in the classrooms.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: The 'local' students take their education quite seriously and for many it is a privilege to be there (and an expensive one!). So respect that when you are there and respect the campus.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Pushing myself to go out and learn new interests and parts of myself - and doing it 'on my own'. Discovering how social and spontanious I can be, engaging in new hobbies and of course, meeting to many new and different people while making great friends.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Balancing having fun, learning new thins and also resting and having down time on your own. Realising not all new people are going to be your friend but pushing yourself to engage with the people you really like.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
